Mental illnesses such as depression has been associated with significant morbidity, mortality, disability, and increased risk of suicide (Khubchandani, Brey, Kotecki, Kleinfelder, & Anderson, 2016). Efforts to increase awareness and screening of depression among college students should be a priority. Local Problem An identified public college health center had a complaint-based approach to depression screening. A complaint-based approach screens for depression if a patient presented with depression-related symptoms. Patients may mask their depressive symptoms and suicidal intent by complaining of other health issues. Patients may report somatic symptoms in an attempt to avoid mental health stigma. Thus, the complaint-based approach may under-detect and under- treat depression. The Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) could be utilized as a first step approach to screen college students for depression during every visit at the college health center. The PHQ-2 has two questions and can easily be administered by healthcare providers at the college health center. College students who screen positive should be further evaluated with the PHQ-9 and possibly referred to counseling services at the identified public college. The counseling center at the identified public college provides an array of mental health services that could be beneficial for college students who are experiencing depression, but college students should first be screened and identified. Clinical Question In college-aged students (P), how does screening for depression with the Patient Health Questionnaire-2 (PHQ-2) (I) compared to current practice (C) affect early identification of depression (O)?

hits.text: DEPRESSION SCREENING IN COLLEGE STUDENTS 5 The Importance of Screening and Early Identification of Depression in College Students In the United States, more than 33.3% of first-year college students reported symptoms that are consistent with a diagnosable mental health disorder, according to the American Psychological Association (Auerbach et al., 2018). Mental health problems among college students have consistently increased over time and it poses a threat to their health and academic performance (Lipson, Lattie, & Eisenberg, 2019). Identification of mental health disorders among college students have been overlooked. Depression is the second most common mental health disorder among college students in the United States (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students are a key population for determining the economic growth and success of the nation. Thus, primary healthcare providers are the front line to early screening and identification of depression amongst college students. Problem Statement The prevalence of depression has risen in the college population in the past decade. There is an estimation of 33.3% of college students exhibiting significant symptoms of depression, generalized anxiety disorder, or suicide ideation (Oswalt et al., 2018). Depression is one of the most common mental health conditions among college students. In the United States, approximately 26% of individuals ages 18 and older live with a diagnosable mental health disorder in a given year (Oswalt et al., 2018). College students with depression can experience a decrease in physical health, negatively impact mental health, hinder relationships, impede academic endeavors, and decrease quality of life (Pedrelli, Nyer, Yeung, Zulauf, & Wilens, 2015). Univer- sity students go through significant changes in their emotional (e.g., loneliness, personal auton- omy) and physical environment (e.g., transition from college to university) [16]. They also deal with the pressure of competition for good grades, carefully plan for future career, participate in extracurricular activities and are more involved in family matters as an adult [17]. Therefore, it is not unexpected for students to be more vulnerable to symptoms of anxiety disorders. Despite high prevalence and potentially severe consequences including decreased quality of life, multiple somatic complaints, maladaptive personality traits, and increased mortality due to suicide, cardiovascular, and cerebrovascular causes, GAD has been largely ignored as a men- tal health condition [18–21]. One important barrier to effective treatment has been inaccurate or no assessment. People who suffer from anxiety disorders are often under-diagnosed and/or treated inadequately [17]. To overcome the hurdles, there is a need for a reliable, valid, and rel- atively brief screening tool for anxiety disorders, particularly for university students. The seven-item Generalized Anxiety Disorder scale (GAD-7) was developed with the purpose of screening for, and assessing the severity of GAD symptoms in both clinical and research con- texts [22]. Conducted on a large primary care sample, the first validation study of GAD-7 found good reliability, as well as criterion, construct, factorial, and procedural validity. Regarding the detection of depression, general practitioners (GPs) hold the key position in most health- care systems: most cases are diagnosed in primary care and most antidepressants are prescribed by GPs.8 Despite the fact that evidence- based treatments are available, few patients receive guideline- based depression care, which could be due to low detection rates in primary care. 14 15 Whereas research has focused on establishing effective treatments for depression, the process of a valid diagnosis and an effective referral process has been fairly neglected.8 Meta- analyses and systematic reviews also conclude that there appears to be insufficient evidence that depression screening alone improves clinical outcomes.11 16 The GET. FEEDBACK.GP multicentre RCT fills in this research gap by testing a novel patient- targeted feedback intervention that aims to increase patient participation and engage- ment in mental healthcare. Trial objectives The multicentre GET.FEEDBACK.GP RCT primarily aims to determine the efficacy of a widely available feed- back intervention after depression screening to reduce depression severity. The primary hypothesis is that patient- targeted feedback leads to a greater reduction in depression severity 6 months after depression screening compared with GP- targeted feedback only or no feed- back. The secondary hypotheses are that patient- targeted feedback is cost- effective and will increase patient engagement in mental healthcare as well as professional depression care according to German guideline recom- mendations
